content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday morning, bringing to a close one of the most closely watched immigration cases of President Donald Trump's second term. The 31-year-old Salvadoran national, whose mistaken deportation to a notorious prison in El Salvador last year drew condemnation from courts and lawmakers alike, landed at Madrid's Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas Airport on a commercial flight, accompanied by his wife and his lawyer, according to Reuters.

Abrego Garcia, wearing a Chicago Bulls cap and sunglasses, left the airport building without speaking to reporters, raising a fist as he climbed into a waiting van, Reuters witnesses reported. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, told reporters in Madrid that his client's departure from the United States as a free man, to a country of his own choosing, was a victory — the outcome Abrego Garcia had been seeking since August 2025.

The case began in March 2025, when US authorities deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador's CECOT megaprison despite a court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution. The error, later acknowledged by the administration, set off a legal battle that reached the US Supreme Court and turned Abrego Garcia into a symbol of the pitfalls of the president's mass deportation campaign. He was eventually brought back to the United States, only to face a second deportation — this time to one of several African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

For months, Abrego Garcia resisted that second removal in court. A federal judge had told him to self-deport by Tuesday, the Associated Press reported, citing a source familiar with the matter. Hours later, a federal court unsealed an order from US District Judge Paula Xinis, issued last week, directing the government to remove his ankle monitor and to permit his "unimpeded departure from the United States," the Wall Street Journal reported.

His lawyers insist the departure is not the end of the story. Sandoval-Moshenberg said the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego Garcia could have legal avenues to return to the United States under a future administration. "Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to last a lot longer than Donald Trump, and he will be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident under the next administration," the lawyer said, according to Reuters.

For now, his status in Spain is far from settled. Abrego Garcia entered the country on a tourist visa, allowing a stay of only up to 90 days, CNN reported. He has not said where he will go next, and his lawyer said he has not decided on a final destination. There was no indication that he entered Spain under any formal agreement with the Spanish authorities, according to NPR.

The Trump administration, for its part, presented the departure as a success. The Department of Homeland Security announced late on Tuesday that Abrego Garcia had self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order, that he had received no incentives and that he would not be allowed back into the United States. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was "delighted" about the departure, repeating the administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia is a gang member — an accusation he has repeatedly denied and which has never been proven in court.

Democrats who championed his case struck a different note. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who travelled to El Salvador earlier this year to meet Abrego Garcia in detention, said the 31-year-old was "travelling to a country of his choice, a free man." In a statement posted on X, Van Hollen said he was relieved Abrego Garcia would be safe "in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration's constant persecution."

The case has resonated well beyond Abrego Garcia himself. His wife and child are both US citizens, and his lawyers say he left because he believed he was "never going to get a fair shake" under the Trump administration despite being married to an American citizen, CNN reported. Legal experts say the saga exposed the limits of judicial oversight of deportations: even after the Supreme Court weighed in, the administration spent months seeking alternative destinations for his removal rather than allowing him to remain with his family in Maryland.

The outcome also highlights how the immigration debate has hardened on both sides of the Atlantic. Governments across Europe have been tightening their own asylum and immigration rules, as [Britain's parliament passed a sweeping immigration and asylum bill this month](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/zh/articles/uk-commons-passes-immigration-asylum-bill-november-2026), extending the wait for permanent residency from five years to ten. In the United States, the administration has continued to defend its deportation programme as essential to public safety, while critics point to Abrego Garcia's case as evidence that the system can sweep up people with lawful claims to remain.

Whether Abrego Garcia eventually returns to the United States remains an open question, and one that may depend as much on American politics as on the law. His lawyers have made clear they view Spain as a staging post, not a final home. For now, though, the man at the centre of a case that tested the presidency, the courts and the country's immigration system is, in his lawyer's words, a free man — and, for the first time in nearly two years, beyond the reach of the administration that tried twice to remove him. [Read Reuters' full report on his arrival in Madrid](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/salvadoran-migrant-kilmar-abrego-garcia-lands-spain-after-us-departure-deal-2026-11-25/)
summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador became a defining test of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States. His lawyers call the move temporary and say he may seek to return under a future administration.
title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Arrives in Spain After Voluntarily Leaving the US, Closing a Two-Year Legal Battle
